title: Trendline Break
teaches: The trendline break as we trade it: a leader above its 200-day drifts tight under a falling line drawn over the daily highs, the buy is the trade through the line and the prior day's high at market in regular hours and never more than 4% past the line, the stop sits a few cents under the trigger day's low, a close back under the line is a warning and not an exit, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a break on its own is a warning, not a reversal.

walkthroughs.title: NUE, October 2006: eight touches, a tight drift
steps: NUE, 2006. Above its 200-day, it pulls back 26% off a 60.30 high. Eight touches over five months draw the line.
It drifts tight under a line 106 sessions long. A higher low forms above the 200-day, and it breaks from there.
October 5 it clears the line, 50.47, on 1.8x volume. Buy at market, 50.48. Stop just under the day's low, 49.20.
The fail is a thin break that closes back under the line. Not here: 3R in 6 sessions. First sell's your call.

walkthroughs.title: MSFT, January 2012: the small honest stop
steps: Even a mega-cap does this. MSFT, January 2012, drifting tight under a five-month line with 6 touches.
A 16% pullback from 28.15, and the last days get quiet: small ranges, closes hugging the line.
January 4 it clears the line, 26.89, and the prior high. Buy at market, 26.97. Stop just under the low, 26.73.
That's a 0.9% stop. If the break fails, you're out small. Instead 3R came the next day.

walkthroughs.title: SCHW, February 2020: the planned loss
steps: Here's one that didn't work. SCHW, February 2020: a clean break of a 46-session line on 1.81x volume.
Buy at market on February 20, 48.12. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 47.25. That's 1.80% risk.

questions.q: You're marking a falling trendline on a pullback the night before. What do you draw it across?
choices: The daily highs, wicks and all
The daily closes, skip the wicks
The lows of the pullback
The 50-day moving average
questions.answer: The daily highs, wicks and all
questions.why: Across the highs, wicks included. A falling line is the sellers' ceiling, so it connects the high points of the pullback. Start at the highest high, where the drop began, and run it across the lower highs after it. The wicks are where sellers actually showed up, so a line over the closes cuts right through them. If you have to fudge it to make it fit, it's not a line.
questions.lesson_line: Highs, wicks and all. Start at the top of the pullback.

wrong.The daily closes, skip the wicks: Closes cut right through the wicks. The wicks are where sellers hit it, so the line goes over them.
wrong.The lows of the pullback: A line under the lows is support. The line you buy a break of sits over the highs.
wrong.The 50-day moving average: That's an average, not a trendline. You draw the line on price itself.

questions.simple: Draw it across the highs, wicks and all, because a falling line connects the high points where sellers stepped in.

questions.q: A stock pokes through its falling line today. On its own, that break is a heads-up, not proof the trend has turned.
questions.why: True. A broken line tells you the selling may be easing. It doesn't tell you buyers have taken over. That's why the stock has to pass our checks first: a leader, holding above its 200-day. Treat every break as a reversal and you'll buy a lot of bounces that roll right back over.

wrong.Line is the setup, flag the backdrop: The run and the rest are the setup. The line is just the door in.
wrong.Wedge pop is the setup, line the trigger: A wedge pop comes after a drop. This stock just ran 25%.

questions.simple: It's a flag, and the line across its top is the trigger, so it's one trade with one stop.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (the flag lookalike)
the standalone-or-trigger question is held (D-002)

questions.q: What are you looking at?
questions.story: A stock closed 12 of the last 15 sessions under its 20 EMA. Then a bar clears a 4-day tight range and both fast averages.
choices: A wedge pop off a decline
A trendline break, it cleared a range
A flat-top break at a ceiling
A launchpad off the averages
questions.answer: A wedge pop off a decline
questions.why: A wedge pop. This stock spent 12 of the last 15 sessions under its 20 EMA. Then it tightened up for 4 days and popped back over both fast averages in one bar. That reclaim is the whole tell. A trendline break looks different: a leader drifting tight under a falling line, then trading through it. Know which one you've got, because each has its own entry and stop.
questions.lesson_line: Lost the averages, then took them back. That's the pop.

wrong.A flat-top break at a ceiling: A flat top is highs stopping at one price. Nothing here says that.
wrong.A trendline break, it cleared a range: The tell here is the averages: lost, then taken back. That's the pop.
wrong.A launchpad off the averages: A launchpad is the averages pinched together, price sitting on them. This one lost them and took them back.

questions.simple: It's a wedge pop, because it sat under the 20 EMA and this bar takes the fast averages back.

reasons: +3 one source only (the card's lookalike lines c40, c41)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Do you take it?
questions.story: The market filter reads Orange: under pressure, one step from Red. A valid break sets up with a stop 6% away and a key level just overhead.
choices: No, it's nowhere near an A+
Yes, the line itself is valid
Yes, but at half size
No, Orange means no new trades
questions.answer: No, it's nowhere near an A+
questions.why: No. In Orange we only take A+ setups, our very best, because breakouts fail more when the market isn't backing them. This isn't close. A 6% stop is past the 5% we'll accept at all, so even in Green I'd wait for a tighter trigger. And a key level right overhead gives it no room. A valid line isn't the same as a good trade.
questions.lesson_line: In Orange, only the very best get through.

wrong.Yes, the line itself is valid: A valid line just gets it on the list. In Orange it has to be an A+.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Half size doesn't turn it into an A+. It's a pass at any size.
wrong.No, Orange means no new trades: Orange still takes the A+ setups. This one just isn't one.

questions.simple: No, because Orange takes only A+ setups, and a wide stop under a key level is nowhere close.

deeper.trap: A valid line is not the same as a good setup. In Orange the question is the grade. A wide stop and a key level just overhead both point away from A+, so it's a pass at any size.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
+1 fixed before (threshold wording removed, E50)

questions.q: How do you handle it?
questions.story: The honest stop, a few cents under the low of the day, sits 4.5% under your buy. Your usual size would risk too much.
choices: Buy fewer shares, or skip it
Tighten the stop to 3% so it fits
Full size, it's only one trade
Buy half now, add the rest later
questions.answer: Buy fewer shares, or skip it
questions.why: Fewer shares, or skip it. The stop comes from the chart, and the size comes from the stop. Shares are your account times your risk percent, divided by the buy minus the stop, rounded down. A 4.5% stop just means fewer shares for the same dollar risk. It's wider than I like, but under 5% I'll take it. Pull the stop up to 3% and normal noise takes you out of a good trade.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Never pull it in to fit.

wrong.Buy half now, add the rest later: We buy the full size once, at one price, with one stop. No buying it in pieces.
wrong.Tighten the stop to 3% so it fits: That's moving the stop to fit the size. The stop stays where the chart says you're wrong.
wrong.Full size, it's only one trade: Full size on a wide stop risks more than you planned. Every trade counts.

questions.simple: Buy fewer shares or skip it, because the stop sets the size, never the other way around.

deeper.example: Say your usual size was built for a stop about 3% away. With the honest stop at 4.5%, the same dollar risk buys about two thirds as many shares. That smaller size is the right size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5) and the card's stop width line

questions.q: Looking back, what was the weak spot in this trade?
questions.story: You bought the break at 18.79 with the stop at 18.53. It closed only 0.39% over the line, on 1.25 times its 50-day average volume. The next day it closed back under the line and the stop traded.
choices: A thin break that barely cleared
The stop was set too tight
You chased past the 4% limit
Line breaks just don't work
questions.answer: A thin break that barely cleared
questions.why: The break itself was thin. It closed just 0.39% over the line, on volume only a bit above normal. Nobody was really pushing. And look at the averages. The 50-day sat under the 200-day, both flat, with price barely over them. No trend to lean on. It slipped back under the line the next day, and the stop took you out small, as planned. Your stop was right where it belongs, and you weren't chasing. Volume raises the grade, and this one had little extra.
questions.lesson_line: A barely-there break is the one that falls back.

wrong.The stop was set too tight: The stop sat a few cents under the low of the day, right where it goes.
wrong.You chased past the 4% limit: You bought at 18.79 with the line at 18.78. Nowhere near a chase.
wrong.Line breaks just don't work: One loss proves nothing. This was a weak break, and the stop kept it small.

questions.simple: The break was thin, barely clearing the line on modest volume, so it fell back and the stop did its job.

reasons: +2 tied to D-069 (volume as a gate or a cue); the key holds under either
+1 fixed before

questions.q: It hasn't hit your stop. Now what?
questions.story: You bought a break 11 trading days ago. It sits at 0.6R after three flat closes and no higher high.
choices: Sell it, it's had its chance
Hold, the stop hasn't traded
Add more, it's holding up
Raise the stop to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it, it's had its chance
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold, and this one's 11 days in at 0.6R. Good breaks tend to go within a few sessions, so no follow-through is the signal. The stop protects you from a loss, not from dead money. Free the money up for the next leader that's actually moving.
questions.lesson_line: No follow-through is the signal. Free up the money.

wrong.Raise the stop to breakeven: Breakeven is for a trade that's paid you. This one hasn't.
wrong.Hold, the stop hasn't traded: The stop guards against a loss, not dead money. The time stop is its own exit.
wrong.Add more, it's holding up: Adding to dead money just ties up more of it. And this one hasn't earned it.

questions.simple: Sell it, because it's still under 1R after 10 trading days, and that money can go to a stock that's moving.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Is it a buy?
questions.story: For three weeks the lows rise into the falling line while volume fades each day. Today it pokes through.
choices: No, it's wedging up into the line
Yes, it broke the line today
Yes, rising lows show demand
No, wait for a close well past it
questions.answer: No, it's wedging up into the line
questions.why: No. Lows rising into a falling line squeeze price into a wedge. That's not the tight drift down we want. It's buyers getting more eager into a ceiling, and a poke through can run out of gas right there. I want price drifting down quietly under the line, with the daily range getting smaller. Then a break means the sellers are done.
questions.lesson_line: Wedging up into the line isn't the drift we want.

wrong.Yes, it broke the line today: Breaking the line isn't enough. What led into it matters.
wrong.Yes, rising lows show demand: Rising lows on fading volume into a ceiling is a wedge, not strength.
wrong.No, wait for a close well past it: We don't wait for a close. We buy the trigger during the day. The shape is why this one's a pass.

questions.simple: No, because lows rising into the line make a wedge, not the quiet drift down we want before a break.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (tl.not_wedging_up)

questions.q: A line break doesn't hand you a price target. So how do you plan to get paid on it?
choices: Sell into strength, then trail
Add the pullback's height on top
Sell it all at the old high
Fixed targets at 2R and 3R
questions.why: Sell some into strength, then trail the rest. The first sell is a judgment call. We very rarely sell on day 1, and most of the time we wait till day 3 at the earliest. Often we sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. What's left rides the 9 or 20 EMA until it closes under it. That way you get paid on the push and still own a piece if it turns into a big leg.
questions.lesson_line: No target. Sell into strength, trail the rest.

wrong.Sell it all at the old high: The old high is supply, not a finish line. Strong ones run right through it.
wrong.Add the pullback's height on top: A measuring rule isn't how we sell. The stock decides how far it goes.
wrong.Fixed targets at 2R and 3R: We don't set fixed 2R and 3R targets. Those cut your winners short.

questions.simple: Sell some into strength by judgment and trail the rest, because a line break gives you no target.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)

deeper.example: Peter Brandt: the violation of a trendline does not carry with it a price target.

questions.q: How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 102 shares. 0.5% of 50,000 is $250 at risk. 109.23 minus 106.79 is 2.44 a share. 250 over 2.44 is 102.46, round down to 102. Then check the cap: no position bigger than 40% of the account, which would be 183 shares here. So 102 stands. The stop picked the size. You just did the math.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: Buy 102 shares, your 250 dollars at risk divided by 2.44 a share, rounded down.

deeper.example: Raise the risk and the share count rises with it. If the count ever makes the position bigger than 40% of the account, the 40% cap sets the size instead.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
+1 fixed before (risk cut from 1% to 0.5% to stay under the cap)

choices: 183 shares
204 shares
102 shares
10,245 shares

wrong.204 shares: That's twice the risk you planned. Use the 0.5%.
wrong.183 shares: That's the 40% cap, the most you could ever own. Your risk sets the size, and it's smaller.
wrong.10,245 shares: You forgot to turn 0.5% into a decimal.

questions.story: Your account is 50,000 and you're risking 0.5% on this one. You bought the break at 109.23 with the stop at 106.79.

questions.q: What's your move with the rest?
questions.story: You've sold twice into strength. What's left is a fast mover. Today it closes under its 9 EMA.
choices: Sell what's left on that close
Hold until the 50-day breaks
Lower the stop to give it room
Wait for the 20 EMA to break
questions.answer: Sell what's left on that close
questions.why: Sell what's left. A fast mover rides the 9 EMA, and it just closed under it. That's the trail doing its job. A fast stock that loses the 9 can give back a lot in a hurry, and you've already been paid twice. Hold for the 20 or the 50 and you hand back gains the trail was built to keep.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Close under it, you're out.

wrong.Hold until the 50-day breaks: Way too loose for a fast mover. The 9 EMA is its line.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up. Never lower it for room.
wrong.Wait for the 20 EMA to break: The 20 EMA is for steadier stocks. A fast mover trails the 9.

questions.simple: Sell what's left, because a fast mover trails the 9 EMA, and it just closed below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52, A4)

questions.q: Your stop got gapped. What now?
questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00. It gaps open at 38.20, and the low of the first 30-minute bar is 37.80.
choices: Out, the loss is 2.2R, past 2R
New stop at 37.80, the 30-min low
Hold, gaps like this fill
New stop at 38.20, the open
questions.why: You're out. On a gap through your stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. But there's a ceiling. Your risk was 40.00 minus 39.00, 1.00 a share. The 30-minute low of 37.80 is 2.20 under your buy, so that's 2.2R. Past 2R, you sell. Take the hit and move on to the next one.
questions.lesson_line: A gapped stop gets 30 minutes, up to 2R. Past that, out.

wrong.New stop at 37.80, the 30-min low: That's the stop only while the loss stays inside 2R. This one's at 2.2R.
wrong.Hold, gaps like this fill: Hoping for a fill isn't a plan. The rule has a ceiling, and this is past it.
wrong.New stop at 38.20, the open: The open isn't the new stop. The first 30-minute low is, and this one's past 2R anyway.

questions.simple: Get out, because the 30-minute low puts the loss at 2.2R, and past 2R the gap rule says sell.

deeper.example: The risk was 40.00 minus 39.00 a share. The first 30-minute low of 37.80 is 2.2 times that under the buy, so the loss is 2.2R. That is past the 2R ceiling, so you are out. Had the low held inside 2R, it would have become the new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 and its ceiling)
computed key (the 2R line)

questions.q: You've been stopped out of the same stock 6 times this month. A fresh trigger shows up today. You can take it if it triggers cleanly.
questions.why: False. On one stock we cap it at 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. You're at 6, so you're done with it until next month. When a stock stops you out that many times, it's telling you something about the stock or the market. Step back. Other names are setting up.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month. Then move on.
questions.simple: False, we cap it at 6 tries a month on one stock, and you've used them all.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E56)
+1 fixed before (replaced a duplicate of q51)

questions.q: Earnings are right there. Do you take the break?
questions.story: A clean break sets up for tomorrow. The company reports after the close in 2 days.
choices: No, the report's inside 3 days
Yes, the line is clean
Yes, and sell before the report
No, it reports this month
questions.why: No. We make no new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this one's in 2. A report can gap a stock right through your stop, and no stop protects you from that. We only hold through earnings when we're already up 5R, so the gap risk is paid for with profit. Put it back on your list for after the report.
questions.lesson_line: Three days before a report, no new buys.

wrong.Yes, the line is clean: A clean line doesn't change the earnings risk.
wrong.Yes, and sell before the report: No new buy in that window at all, even a quick one.
wrong.No, it reports this month: It's narrower than that. Just no new buys in the 3 days before a report.

questions.simple: No, we make no new buys in the 3 days before a report. A report can gap right through your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Your stock's going straight up. How do you play it?
questions.story: You're up 2.5R after three days of a vertical, wide-range climb.
choices: Sell a big part into strength
Add more, it's going parabolic
Hold it all, let the trail work
Raise the stop to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell a big part into strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Three days of wide, vertical bars is a climax run. That's buyers chasing, and you get to sell to them. How much is a judgment call, but make it a real piece. Then let the rest ride the trail. Adding here is the worst move. You'd be buying the top off someone else's excitement.
questions.lesson_line: A vertical burst is for selling into.

wrong.Raise the stop to breakeven: Moving the stop protects your buy, not the gains. Sell some here.
wrong.Add more, it's going parabolic: Never add into a climax. You'd be buying the top.
wrong.Hold it all, let the trail work: A climax is when you sell into strength, not when you leave it all to the trail.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into strength, because a vertical climb hands you eager buyers to sell to.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Do you sell any here?
questions.story: You bought the break at 144.71 with the stop at 142.42. On day 2 it trades up to 3R.
choices: Hold, and raise the stop to breakeven
Sell a third, 3R is the rule
Sell half and trail the rest
Sell it all, 3R is the target
questions.answer: Hold, and raise the stop to breakeven
questions.why: Hold, and raise the stop to breakeven at 144.71. 3R in two days is a strong start. But it's day 2, and we very rarely sell that early. Most of the time we wait till day 3 at the earliest, often selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. 3R sits inside our 2R to 5R window for breakeven. With the stop at your buy, a fast winner can't turn into a loser. One honest note on this chart. Your 144.71 fill sat just under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks under it. The right buy waited until it cleared the 200-day. It did that same day.
questions.lesson_line: 3R on day 2. Raise the stop and keep it.

wrong.Sell a third, 3R is the rule: 3R is a ruler, not a sell signal. And it's only day 2.
wrong.Sell half and trail the rest: Half on day 2 cuts a strong winner off early.
wrong.Sell it all, 3R is the target: 3R isn't a target. Strong ones like this can run a lot further.

questions.simple: Hold and move the stop to breakeven, because it's only day 2 and we rarely sell that soon.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
computed key (33.00 is 3R)

questions.q: You followed every rule. What was the loss?
questions.story: You bought through an 83-session line at 18.79 with the stop at 18.53. The break closed only 0.39% over the line. Next day the low was 18.39.
choices: A planned loss; the stop did its job
A mistake; the stop was too tight
A reason to redraw the line
questions.answer: A planned loss; the stop did its job
questions.why: A planned loss. The stop is the exit and it did its job. A break that barely clears the line is a weak one.
questions.lesson_line: A stop that trades is the plan working.

wrong.A mistake; the stop was too tight: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low by the rule. Widening it to dodge a loss is the mistake.
wrong.A reason to redraw the line: Redrawing the line to get back in is the named mistake. Only a new trigger buys again.

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: You bought at 145.75 with the stop at 144.17, so 3R is 150.49 and 5R is 153.65. The next session opens at 152.00.
choices: Sell a third at the open
Hold; wait for the close
Sell it all at the open
Sell two thirds at the open
questions.answer: Sell a third at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. Our rule: if a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. The open at 152.00 is past 3R at 150.49, so the first third goes at once. That session then fell to 144.06 and the stop took the rest. The trim had already banked a gain.
questions.lesson_line: Take the trim the open hands you.

wrong.Hold; wait for the close: The level is already passed. Waiting gave the gap time to fill.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: A third at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Sell two thirds at the open: The open at 152.00 is past 3R at 150.49 but short of 5R at 153.65. Only the first third comes off.

questions.simple: Sell a third right at the open, because the price opened past the 3R trim level, so the trim is already due.

deeper.example: This is EL in December 2018. The buy was 145.75 with the stop at 144.17. The next session opened at 152.00, past 3R, then fell to 144.06, under the stop. Waiting for the close would have handed the whole gap back. The trim at the open banked a third at a profit before the stop took the rest.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)
computed key (3R level in the story)

questions.q: Where is the buy?
questions.story: A stock forms a high tight flag after a sharp run. A falling line crosses the flag's highs.
choices: Over the pattern's highest high
Through the falling line at once
On a dip to the 50-day average
At the flag's low, on weakness
questions.why: Over the pattern's highest high. Our card names this mistake: using the flag's trendline break on a high tight flag. Citing Bulkowski, it says they fail too often that way. A plain flag can use its line as the trigger; a high tight flag buys its highest high.
questions.lesson_line: On a high tight flag, buy the pattern high, not the line.

wrong.Through the falling line at once: On a high tight flag the flag's trendline break fails too often. That is the named mistake.
wrong.At the flag's low, on weakness: Buying the flag's low is buying weakness with no trigger. The buy is on strength, over the pattern's highest high.
wrong.On a dip to the 50-day average: Our buy is on strength over the pattern's highest high, not on a dip to an average.

questions.simple: Buy over the pattern's highest high, because breaks of the flag's line fail too often on a high tight flag.

deeper.trap: A falling line across a flag looks like a trendline break, and the first push through it is tempting. On a high tight flag that early buy fails too often. Wait for price to clear the highest high of the whole pattern.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (c43; Bulkowski's line is the card's, not quoted from his page)
+2 tied to D-002 (the setup map)

questions.q: You got shaken out and then it ripped. What now?
questions.story: You bought at 200.06 with the stop at 197.41. The next day's low was 197.22, 19 cents under your stop, and it closed at 209.53.
choices: Wait for a new trigger
Buy it back now, it ran 6%
Re-enter, you get 3 tries
Redraw the line, buy back in
questions.why: Wait for a new trigger. This one stings. The low missed your stop by 19 cents, then it closed at 209.53. But your stop did exactly what it's for. After a stop-out we only buy back when the setup triggers again. That's a brand new trade with its own stop and size. Chase it here and you're paying way up with no level to lean on. It reached 217 within a week. That's the cost of having a stop. Pay it and wait for your spot.
questions.lesson_line: It ran without you. Only a new trigger buys it back.

wrong.Buy it back now, it ran 6%: Chasing what ran is how one loss turns into two.
wrong.Re-enter, you get 3 tries: Three tries a week is a cap, not a free pass. Each one needs a new trigger.
wrong.Redraw the line, buy back in: Redrawing the line to get back in is making up a level. Only a new trigger counts.

questions.simple: Wait for a new trigger, because after a stop-out we only buy again when the setup fires again as a new trade.

deeper.trap: The pain is real: the stop missed by 19 cents and the stock ran to 217 without you. The trap is to fix that feeling by chasing, by redrawing the line, or by treating the 3 tries as free entries. Each one breaks a rule. Only a new trigger brings you back, with its own stop and size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)
the structural stop is held (D-008) and never keyed

questions.q: What does the quiet volume say?
questions.story: A clean line of 3 touches over 85 sessions breaks, but on only 0.86x the 50-day average volume.
choices: Weak; a break with volume matters more
Nothing; volume is noise
Strong; no one is selling
questions.answer: Weak; a break with volume matters more
questions.why: Weak. A trendline break with volume matters more than a break without. This quiet one is a poor sign.
questions.lesson_line: Volume confirms the break. A quiet break is a weak one.

wrong.Nothing; volume is noise: The Insider says a break with volume matters more than one without.
wrong.Strong; no one is selling: Quiet volume on a break is not strength. Buyers did not show up.

questions.q: It's through the line. Are you buying?
questions.story: A steep three-week drop leaves two lower highs. A line through them breaks today.
choices: No, it's a drop, not a tight drift
Yes, the line broke today
Yes, but on half the size
No, lower highs mean downtrend
questions.answer: No, it's a drop, not a tight drift
questions.why: No. A steep three-week drop isn't a tight drift. It's a drop. A line drawn off a fast plunge is steep, and steep lines break easily without meaning much. The stock just stopped falling so hard. I want a slow drift down under a shallow line, where sellers dry up over weeks. That's the break that tells me the selling is really done.
questions.lesson_line: A steep plunge draws a steep line. Skip it.

wrong.Yes, the line broke today: Breaking a steep line is easy. It doesn't mean the selling is done.
wrong.Yes, but on half the size: Size doesn't fix a bad setup. A steep line off a plunge is still a pass.
wrong.No, lower highs mean downtrend: Lower highs make any falling line. The problem here is how steep it is.

questions.simple: No, because a steep line off a fast drop breaks easily and means little, and we want a slow tight drift.

deeper.counter: Compare a real line from our research. MSFT in 2012 drifted tight under a line with 6 touches over 112 sessions, and 3R came the next day. That's a slow drift. This story is a plunge with two lower highs.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (the steep-line mistake)
the slope number is held (D-069) and never keyed

questions.q: Did you do something wrong?
questions.story: You buy a clean break at 48.12 with the stop at 47.25. The next session is the first day of a market break, and the stop trades.
choices: No, a planned loss, rules kept
Yes, should've waited a day
Yes, the stop was too wide
No, so rebuy at the same price
questions.answer: No, a planned loss, rules kept
questions.why: No. You took a planned loss, and the stop did its job. The risk was 48.12 minus 47.25, about 1.8% of your buy. The next day was the first day of the February 2020 market break, and nobody reads that off a daily chart. A valid break can still lose. What matters is that it lost small. The stock was at 34.45 within 10 sessions. Without that stop you'd have been down a lot more.
questions.lesson_line: A good trade can lose. The stop keeps it small.

wrong.Yes, should've waited a day: Waiting would've been a different trade. This one followed the plan.
wrong.Yes, the stop was too wide: About 1.8% is a tight stop, well inside where we like it.
wrong.No, so rebuy at the same price: Right verdict, wrong next step. You buy again only on a new trigger.

questions.simple: No, the stop did its job, so the loss was small and planned.

deeper.counter: The stock fell to 34.45 within 10 sessions. Without the stop, the loss would have been far bigger than the 1.80% planned. A rule that loses small on a bad day has done its work.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: In our test the stop never moved and nothing was sold early. Many reached 3R first, yet 78.8% ended at the stop. What's the fix?
choices: Sell into strength, then trail
Stop trading line breaks
Widen the stop to stay in longer
Drop the stop, let winners run
questions.why: Sell into strength, then trail. Look at what happened. A lot of these breaks reached 3R before the stop, and still 78.8% ended up stopped out. The entries worked. The exits gave it back. Nothing was ever sold and the stop never moved, so most winners rode all the way back to it. So we sell some into strength, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Then we trail the rest under the 9 or 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Get paid on the push. Trail the rest.

wrong.Stop trading line breaks: Plenty reached 3R first. The entries were fine. The exits weren't.
wrong.Widen the stop to stay in longer: A wider stop just loses more. The problem was never selling.
wrong.Drop the stop, let winners run: No stop means no plan for a loser. Keep it, and sell into strength.

questions.q: Write your plan. Where's the stop, and when's the first sell?
questions.story: This is the day before. Tomorrow it trades through its falling line at 39.25 and the prior day's high. You fill at 39.26. The low of the day is 38.89.
choices: Stop under 38.89, sell day 3 or later
Stop on the line, sell day 3 or later
Stop under 38.89, sell a third day 1
Stop on the line, sell a third day 1
questions.answer: Stop under 38.89, sell day 3 or later
questions.why: Stop a few cents under 38.89, and no selling before day 3. The line at 39.25 is your trigger, not your stop. If the low of the day breaks, the break failed, so that's where the stop goes. That's a tight one, well inside where we like it. Then you sit. We very rarely sell on day 1, and most of the time we wait till day 3 at the earliest. Give it room to push.
questions.lesson_line: Stop under the low of the day. Sell later, not on day 1.

wrong.Stop on the line, sell day 3 or later: 39.25 is the line, your trigger. The stop goes under the low of the day.
wrong.Stop under 38.89, sell a third day 1: The stop's right, but we very rarely sell on day 1.
wrong.Stop on the line, sell a third day 1: Both miss. Stop under the low of the day, and no selling on day 1.

questions.simple: Stop a few cents under 38.89, not on the line, and hold off selling until day 3 or later.

deeper.trap: A stop on the line feels logical, since the line is what broke. But the line is the trigger, not the stop. The stop is a price a few cents under the trigger day's low.

questions.q: Which one gets the bigger position?
questions.story: Two valid breaks, months apart. A: a leader tight under the line, room overhead, stop 1.5% away, Green market. B: stop 4% away, a key level just above, Yellow market.
choices: A, everything lines up
B, it has the wider stop
Equal, the line is the same
Equal, the stop sets the size
questions.why: A, and by a lot. A is the spot I want: tight under the line, room to run, a 1.5% stop, and a Green market behind it. B has a key level right on top, a 4% stop and a Yellow market, which means smaller and fewer. At the same dollar risk, B's wider stop already buys fewer shares. Then the grade and the market cut it again. Size up where everything lines up.
questions.lesson_line: Same line, different spot. The spot and the market set the size.

wrong.B, it has the wider stop: A wider stop means fewer shares, not more.
wrong.Equal, the line is the same: The line's the same. The market, the stop and the room aren't.
wrong.Equal, the stop sets the size: The stop sets the size, and B's 4% stop already means fewer shares than A's 1.5%.

questions.simple: A gets more, because it's tight with room in a Green market, while B has a wider stop in a Yellow one.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a valid break is a valid break. Both lines qualify, so the line doesn't decide the size. The stock's spot and the market do.

questions.q: Is this the first break?
questions.story: Last week a stock closed over its falling line, then slid back under. Today it trades through the line again.
choices: No; it already closed through
Yes; a wick is allowed
Yes; each day starts fresh
No; a week is too soon
questions.why: No. A first break has no daily close above the line between the first anchor and the trigger day. A wick through is allowed, a close is not. The close last week spent the first break.
questions.lesson_line: One close over the line spends the first break.

wrong.Yes; a wick is allowed: A wick is allowed, but a close above the line is not. This one closed over it.
wrong.Yes; each day starts fresh: The rule counts closes above the line since the first anchor, not days.
wrong.No; a week is too soon: Our card's rule is about closes, not waiting. One daily close above the line already spent the first break.

questions.simple: No, because the stock already closed above the line last week, and a first break has no earlier close above it.

deeper.trap: A close over the line, a slide back under, then a fresh push can look like a second chance. By the card it is a line already spent. It is not a first break, so it is not this setup's buy.

questions.why: False. The old high is overhead supply, context and not a rule. No pattern target replaces the R-based trims.

questions.q: Nice line. Is it worth buying?
questions.story: A clean break of a long falling line, in a stock with an RS rating of 55 and a group that's lagging.
choices: No, it's not a leader
Yes, the line is clean
Yes, with a tighter stop and size
No, a line that long is stale
questions.why: No. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A 55 in a lagging group is a stock the market doesn't care about right now. The line can be perfect and it'll still lag when the real leaders go. Check the stock before you draw the line. The RS Rating is right there in our app.
questions.lesson_line: The stock comes before the line.

wrong.Yes, the line is clean: A clean line in a weak stock is still a weak stock.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop and size: A tighter stop doesn't make a laggard a leader.
wrong.No, a line that long is stale: Length isn't the problem. The RS is.

questions.simple: No, because we only buy leaders with an RS of 80 or more, and this one's at 55 in a lagging group.

deeper.counter: A clean line in a weak stock is the classic trap. The chart looks right, so the stock gets a pass. Run the stock first: $10 or more and $20 million a day. It closes above the 200-day, with an RS of 80 or more in a strong group. Only then look at the line.

questions.q: A leader drifts tight under lower highs, and its falling line sits right around 610. Check the 200-day. Take the break or pass?
choices: Take it, it's above the 200-day
Pass, it's under the 200-day
Pass, the share price is too high
Take it, then add on a dip
questions.why: Take it. Price is holding above the 200-day, so it passes the first check. Then look at the drift: tight, right under a shallow line of lower highs, right around 610. That's what I want. This is MCK in February 2025. It triggered at 609.84 with the stop at 601.40, about 1.4% away, and ran straight to new highs. One buy, full size, one stop.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day first, then the drift, then the line.

wrong.Pass, it's under the 200-day: Look again. Price is above the 200-day here.
wrong.Pass, the share price is too high: A high price isn't a reason to pass. What matters is $10 or more and $20 million a day.
wrong.Take it, then add on a dip: Adding on a dip is never the plan. Full size once, one stop.

questions.simple: Take it, because it's above its 200-day and drifting tight under a slow falling line.

deeper.example: A slow line is still a line. It falls a little from lower highs, so it's not a flat top. Five touches on it made it easy to see.

reasons: rests on our own research data (one dossier) and the settled 200-day rule

questions.q: The highs have stepped lower for months, each one turned back on the same slope. Check the 200-day. Take the break or pass?
choices: Pass, it's under the 200-day
Take it, the line is long and clean
Take it, the volume looks fine
Pass, the line isn't steep enough
questions.why: Pass. It's sitting well under its 200-day, and the 50 is under the 200 and still pointing down. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line. A stock down there is still working off a downtrend, and a nice run of lower highs is just a bounce in a weak stock. Even on the break the next day, it closed 4.9% under its 200-day. Check the 200-day before you even draw the line.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, it's a pass, however nice the line.

wrong.Take it, the line is long and clean: A clean line doesn't matter if the stock's under the 200-day.
wrong.Take it, the volume looks fine: Volume doesn't lift a stock over its 200-day.
wrong.Pass, the line isn't steep enough: Steeper isn't better. Steep lines mean less. The 200-day is the problem.

questions.simple: Pass. It's well under its 200-day, and below the 200-day we don't buy stocks.

deeper.trap: A long line with clean touches pulls the eye. Check the 200-day first. If the stock closes under it, the line doesn't matter for a long.

questions.q: You've got room for one. Which do you take?
questions.story: Four breaks today. A: under its 200-day. B: reports in 2 days. C: a leader, tight under the line. D: gaps 5% over the line.
choices: A, the 200-day is a soft rule
B, just sell it before the report
C, nothing rules it out
D, the gap shows strength
questions.why: C. Every other one fails something. A is under its 200-day, and we don't buy stocks down there. B reports in 2 days, inside the 3 days before a report when we make no new buys. D gapped 5% over the line, past the 4% we'll ever pay. C is a leader tight under its line, and nothing here rules it out. Run the checks first, then get excited.
questions.lesson_line: Run every check. One fail ends it.

wrong.A, the 200-day is a soft rule: The 200-day is a hard line for stocks. A nice line doesn't change that.
wrong.B, just sell it before the report: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Selling early doesn't change that.
wrong.D, the gap shows strength: 5% over the line is past our 4%. That's a chase, however strong it looks.

questions.simple: C, because each of the others breaks a rule: under the 200-day, a report in 2 days, or a gap past 4%.

deeper.trap: The trap is ranking them by excitement. D's 5% gap looks strongest, but it's past the 4% line, so buying it is a chase. Run the checks first, then pick from what's left.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, B26, C28) and the card

questions.q: The classic books wait for a close 3% past the line before buying. We wait for that close too.
questions.why: False. We buy the trigger during the day, as price trades through the line. We don't wait for any close, let alone one 3% past it. That 3% close was built for long-term lines. On ours, waiting for it uses up most of the 4% we'll pay over the line. It also pushes your stop farther away. You'd be buying late with fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: We buy the trigger. We don't wait for the close.
questions.simple: False, we buy as it trades through the line during the day, so we don't wait for a close 3% past it.

questions.q: If you wait and buy that close, what changes for you?
choices: Fewer shares for the same risk
More risk on the trade, same shares
A tighter stop and more shares
Nothing, only the price is higher
questions.story: Price trades through the line today. A book says to wait for a close 3% past the line before buying.
questions.answer: Fewer shares for the same risk
questions.why: Fewer shares. Your stop still sits under the low of the day, down near the line. Buy 3% higher and the gap from your buy to your stop gets wider. Your dollar risk stays the same, so the share count shrinks. That's what chasing costs you: size, not risk. And it eats most of the 4% we'll ever pay over the line. Buy the trigger instead.
questions.lesson_line: Waiting for the close costs you shares.

wrong.More risk on the trade, same shares: Your dollar risk stays the same. The shares shrink instead.
wrong.A tighter stop and more shares: It's the reverse. A higher buy widens the stop, so you get fewer shares.
wrong.Nothing, only the price is higher: A higher buy with the same stop widens the gap. Fewer shares.

questions.simple: Fewer shares, because a higher buy puts your stop farther away, and your dollar risk stays the same.

deeper.counter: The classic 3% close was built for long-term lines, where a small poke through can mean little. We buy the trigger, and we never pay more than 4% over the line. A 3% wait uses up most of that room before you even buy.
